strengths: The approach addresses a useful computational problem: predicting dual potentials provides a practical warm start while retaining Sinkhorn refinement. Combining supervised potential prediction with adversarially generated training distributions is well motivated.

The reported gains are consistent across random distributions, Quick Draw, MNIST, and CIFAR. Tables 1–2 show approximately 16% and 33% fewer iterations on average at marginal-error thresholds of 10⁻³ and 10⁻², respectively. Runtime and transport-error plots provide complementary evidence.
Training on generated distributions and transferring to several real datasets is promising evidence of generalization beyond a particular training dataset.

The manuscript provides understandable algorithms, network architectures, training hyperparameters, and a code link. Proposition 7 supplies a valid bound on the entropic dual objective under the stated positive-marginal setting.
weaknesses: The principal methodological contribution is insufficiently isolated. There is no ablation against a frozen generator or ordinary synthetic sampling with matched training budgets. Downstream convergence experiments compare only against all-ones initialization, omitting the cited learned and analytic warm starts. Consequently, the results establish improvement over the default but do not establish the value of adversarial generation or its advantage over relevant prior work. This is the main concern behind my recommendation.

Figure 3 evaluates the alternative dual-objective training loss using potential MSE. Lower MSE does not necessarily imply better initialization, and the manuscript does not clarify gauge alignment despite potentials being invariant to additive shifts. A direct comparison of resulting Sinkhorn convergence and runtime is needed to support the claimed superiority of supervised training.

The claim of generalization to arbitrary distributions is substantially broader than the evidence. All experiments use 28×28 images, the same squared-Euclidean cost, one regularization value, and positivity smoothing. These demonstrate useful transfer within a restricted setting, but do not establish universality, robustness to concentrated distributions, or effectiveness across regularization strengths.

Proposition 7 bounds objective suboptimality, not distance between regularized and unregularized potentials or subsequent Sinkhorn convergence. Its mnε bound is approximately 153.7 in the experimental setting, making it uninformative at the reported cost scale. The interpretation in Section 3.3 therefore exceeds what the proposition establishes, although this does not invalidate the empirical gains.

The standalone barycenter claim is supported only by visual examples. There is no reference solver comparison, objective-error measurement, or quantitative runtime evaluation. The assumed zero-mean prediction errors are not established, and unbiased objective estimates at fixed inputs would not by themselves justify accurate gradients or minimizers.

Experimental reporting leaves important uncertainties: test-pair counts, independent training runs, confidence-interval construction, and numerical stabilization at the very small regularization value are unspecified. The approximately three-hour training cost also lacks an amortization analysis, limiting assessment of practical savings.
